17.0.0.en: 1- “Hear the right, O Lord; attend unto my cry; give ear unto my prayer, that goeth not out of feigned lips.”

17.0.1.en: 1- Since David finds injustice surrounding him, he looks to God, who is the Truth, confident that He rejects injustice because He is perfect in His justice, and he entreats Him to hear his complaint, which is a righteous one against the slanders and wrongs of his enemies.

17.0.2.en: 2- David pours out feelings from the depths of his being because he is suffering and wronged, so his prayer goes up to God like a cry.

17.0.3.en: 3- David affirms that his words and entreaties are pure before God, in contrast to the lies of his enemies, who have risen up against him.

17.0.4.en: 4- David's faith in God appears in his persistence, as he repeats his cry and entreaties to God three times in this verse and throughout the Psalm when he says (hear, attend, give ear). His persistence also expresses how much he is suffering from injustice, and his asking God to turn to him and to give attention to the details of his prayer. Perhaps he is addressing the Holy Trinity, asking for help from God in all His hypostases.

17.0.5.en: 5- David trusts that God loves righteousness and answers the prayers of the righteous, for “the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (Jas 5:16). So he tells God that his prayer comes from “lips without deceit”, and by this he of course does not mean to boast.

17.0.6.en: 6- This verse applies fully only to Christ, the Righteous and Holy One, whose lips are without hypocrisy, for it is He who said, “Which of you convinceth me of sin?” (Jn 8:46). Here Christ intercedes for His whole Church as its representative before God the Father, to remove from it the injustice of Satan.

17.1.0.en: 2- “Let my sentence come forth from thy presence; let thine eyes behold the things that are equal.”

17.1.1.en: 1- David believes that God alone is the Judge of the whole world, and that all the judgments of men are void without God. So David's judgment comes forth from before God, and this makes David firm, so that he is not shaken by the lies of the wicked, however many or persuasive they may seem, because God searches the hearts and the reins, and everything is naked and open before Him; and, on the other hand, He shows partiality to no one.

17.1.2.en: 2- God the Holy sees only the things that are upright, and rejects the crooked deeds of men. Therefore David is sure that God will look upon the uprightness of his conduct and deliver him from the wicked.

17.1.3.en: 3- Because David loved God and clung to Him, he wishes that his words and his judgments, that is, his judgment of his people as a king, would come forth from before God. David truly has a heart like God's heart, and wants his will to be God's will, and consequently his eyes see only the things that are upright, as appears in the Septuagint translation, which says, “my eyes behold the things that are upright.”

17.1.4.en: 4- The Septuagint translation says, “from before Thy face let my judgment come forth.” The face of God is Christ: “No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him” (Jn 1:18). Christ is the just Judge and the Judge on the Day of Judgment (Jn 5:22).

17.1.5.en: 5- When David asks for God's judgment, he trusts that His judgment is for the good of his enemies and not for their harm; even if God's judgment contains discipline for the enemies, it is so that they may repent and be saved. David loves his enemies and seeks their good when he asks for judgment from the face of God.

17.2.0.en: 3- “Thou hast proved mine heart; thou hast visited me in the night; thou hast refined me, and shalt find no blame in me; my mouth shall not transgress.”

17.2.2.en: Blame: evil; it comes from the verb “to blame.”

17.2.3.en: 1- David, who gives his life to God and submits to His commandments, examines himself every night, and finds that God through His commandments examines him and alerts him to his iniquities, so that he may repent of them and God may cleanse him from all evil.

17.2.4.en: 2- David does not review himself only concerning his deeds and words, but also concerning the feelings of his heart and his inner intentions. God tries him every night, that is, God constantly visits him with examination through the accounting of the soul, and this shows that David always lives in repentance and purity; therefore his prayer, which comes from a pure heart, is made entirely of pure words. It seems that he spent a long part of the night in this repentance, because he says, “thou hast visited me in the night”: if he spent the day at work, he spent the night in repentance and in meditation on God's commandments in order to be pure.

17.2.5.en: 3- David speaks with confidence to God, who purifies him every night, and he declares that there is no evil or wickedness within him. Yet he is not speaking with pride; rather he shows how perfect God's work is in purifying him. And in the sixth Psalm he affirms his deep repentance every night, saying, “I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears” (Ps 6:6).

17.2.6.en: 4- When God tries a person, He examines him thoroughly, so that he becomes utterly pure. Here David attributes the purification to God when he says, “Thou hast proved mine heart,” so that the result is assured, namely purity.

17.2.7.en: 5- He who is occupied by the lusts of the world during the day has his night filled with evil thoughts and dreams; but he who sets the Lord always before him (Ps 16:8), like David, spends his night with God. He hears His voice, which visits him and alerts him to repent, and he feels God's kindnesses and thanks Him, so that the night becomes a greater delight to him than the day, since his heart is free for prayer, as the holy Fathers said, “The night is set apart for prayer.”

17.2.8.en: 6- God's visiting David is not only at night, but also during the day.

17.2.9.en: 7- If an evil thought comes to David's mind, he drives it away at once and does not let it come out in words; therefore he says, “my mouth shall not transgress.”

17.2.10.en: 8- In humility David attributes the whole purification to God when he says, “Thou hast proved mine heart,” then “thou hast visited me in the night,” and after that “thou hast refined me,” that is, You have examined me with all precision in hard trials, as gold is purified from impurities by fire, and You found me in the end pure: “thou shalt find no blame in me.” Consequently he beseeches God to hear him and deliver him from the wicked oppressors.

17.2.11.en: 9- We notice that David does not speak of the evils of his enemies, but prays with a pure heart in which there is no blame toward any person. This is one of the conditions of accepted prayer, the remaining conditions of which we notice in the verses of the whole Psalm: he condemns no one, and he prays with a heart that bears no resentment against those who wronged him; therefore God hears his prayer.

17.3.0.en: 4- “Concerning the works of men, by the word of thy lips I have kept me from the paths of the destroyer.”

17.3.1.en: The violent one: the harsh and cruel.

17.3.2.en: 1- This verse shows David's concern for the words of God's lips, that is, His commandments; he meditates on them, obeys them, and lets them lead his life in his conduct with others.

17.3.3.en: 2- He is not disturbed by the works of violent men who wrong him or others, but remains in his upright conduct according to God's commandments. He loves everyone and is not overcome by evil, but overcomes evil with good; the credit for David's upright works goes back to the word of God.

17.3.4.en: 3- David enjoys a pure tongue, as he said in (v. 1) “from lips without deceit,” and likewise a pure heart (v. 3), for God proved his heart and found in it no “blame.” In this verse he tells us about his pure works, which are according to God's commandments, even if he lives among the wicked, the hard of heart, and is not influenced by their ways and conduct.

17.3.5.en: 4- Even if the ways of the violent wicked carry evil speech against David, David the righteous was not driven to speak evil words against them or about them, because he is obedient to the word of God, who keeps him from evil. The word of God keeps the tongue of His righteous children, so that they do not slip into evil, even if the wicked say evil things about them.

17.4.0.en: 5- “Hold up my goings in thy paths, that my footsteps slip not.”

17.4.1.en: 1- What are the footsteps of God but His works with mankind and in nature, all of which is good and for edification? David admired these footsteps, so he walked after God to do good to every person, even the wicked among them.

17.4.2.en: 2- In this verse we see David's attachment to God and his trust, as a son, in holding fast to God's footsteps; he cannot walk on a road without God, that is, without God being a leader for him and a light for his path.

17.4.3.en: 3- David's following after God kept him from following after evil, and consequently he was not exposed to slipping and falling into the sins of the wicked around him.

17.4.4.en: 4- God's love appears in His care for His righteous children, as He places signs on the spiritual road that leads to the Kingdom, so that His children may walk by their guidance, and these are His footsteps. God does not leave Himself without witness (Acts 14:17), such as the righteous and the just who live among us, and likewise everything that happens in the events around us; even the wrongs that others do to us may be a sign on the road, that we may take heed not to slip into sin.

17.4.5.en: 5- In the Septuagint translation it says, “Establish my goings,” instead of “my footsteps hold fast.” From this appears David's request for God's help, which establishes him on the road; even if the road is hard, he is able to cross it with God's help, and indeed to be firm on the divine road, not turning aside from it through the wiles of the devil.

17.4.6.en: 6- This verse is a prophecy about the footsteps of Christ, who became incarnate and lived in our midst so that we might follow Him in all His life, as it appears in the four Gospels.

17.5.0.en: 6- “I have called upon thee, for thou wilt hear me, O God: incline thine ear unto me, and hear my speech.”

17.5.1.en: 1- David believes in God's fatherhood, and that He hears him and answers him, because He is also able to answer; therefore he calls upon Him and asks of Him all his needs in prayer, and he also trusts in His justice, for He does not accept injustice.

17.5.2.en: 2- David likewise trusts in God's love and humility, and asks Him to condescend and incline His ear to his prayers. He knows that he has a place in God's heart which no one else fills, and trusts that God cares for him and hears his requests.

17.5.3.en: 3- David has tested God in his life, for he sought Him often and He answered him; this gives him confidence and boldness to call upon Him today.

17.5.4.en: 4- God's inclining His ear appears clearly in the Incarnation of His only Son, to declare His nearness to us and His care for our needs. Therefore this verse is a prophecy about Christ, because Christ is our Intercessor, since through His redemption our requests reach the Father.

17.6.0.en: 7- “Show thy marvellous lovingkindness, O thou that savest by thy right hand them which put their trust in thee from those that rise up against them.”

17.6.1.en: 1- David, who trusts in God's mercy, asks for distinguished and wondrous mercies for those who trust in God like himself, since he has none but God to support him, whereas the wicked adversaries rely on the powers of the world, that is, their influence, their money and their great numbers; and God in His wisdom and justice pours out countless mercies on those who trust in Him.

17.6.2.en: 2- David trusts in God's mercy, so he asks that these mercies be from His right hand, that is, from the fullness of His power, so that they may be wondrous and great mercies, which will of course support those who trust in Him.

17.6.3.en: 3- David asks God to answer his prayers because He is the Truth and Justice (v. 1), and also because He is righteous and so cares for the pure (v. 3); and then, thirdly, he asks that his prayers be answered by the merciful God, who has great mercy on those who trust in Him (v. 6).

17.6.4.en: 4- God's right hand is a symbol of Christ, who sat at the right hand of the Father; here it is a symbol of the Incarnation of Christ, who has mercy on the believers who trust in God through His redemption.

17.6.5.en: 5- David asks God to distinguish His mercies, meaning to show them clearly, lest some people think that they happen by chance and not from God. He wants all people to know that God is the source of mercies, and that He uses people and the events of life as instruments to show His mercies; but here David wants God's mercies to be so distinguished that a person cannot overlook them or doubt them, like the standing still of the sun for Joshua during his war (Josh 10:13), or the going back of the shadow to declare God's mercy in extending the life of King Hezekiah by fifteen years (Isa 38:8).

17.6.6.en: 6- God's right hand, which supports a person and protects him, does not prevent the wars of the adversaries, but it supports him so that he overcomes them. In life we will meet trials, but our Christ promises us that “In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world” (Jn 61:33).

17.7.0.en: 8- “Keep me as the apple of the eye, hide me under the shadow of thy wings,”

17.7.1.en: Apple (pupil): the round opening in the middle of the iris of the eye, which appears black but is transparent; light enters the eye through it, and it is in the center of the eye.

17.7.2.en: 1- David is reassured by God's care and tenderness, so he asks Him to look after him and keep him, and he trusts in God's precise care, which looks after his weakness, as a person looks after his eye and closes his eyelids over it so that it is not exposed to dust or any foreign bodies. So God keeps him from every evil and from any problems greater than he, and shuts him in His embrace, so that he is at peace however much troubles surround him. God makes him close his eyes to evil sights, and feel God's works in everything good around him.

17.7.3.en: 2- In humility David feels his weakness and asks for God's protection, which covers him with His wings, so that the sun, which is a symbol of trials, does not scorch him. In God's shadow he feels protection and peace, as the hen protects her chicks with her wings (Mt 23:37).

17.7.4.en: 3- David trusts in his sonship to God, that is, God's love for him as a father for his son, and even higher than this, for he feels that he is the apple of God's eye (Zech 2:8), which He keeps with His care; and by this confidence of love he receives abundant blessings and care from God.

17.7.5.en: 4- God created the human eye amid bones that surround it, called the socket of the eye, to protect the eye from any external injury. The eye is a very important organ in the body, through which a person sees all that is around him and so leads the whole body in the right way. God's care for the eye is care for the whole body, and God's care for David is care for all his people, because he is their shepherd.

17.7.6.en: 5- God's keeping of the apple of the eye is to make it a single eye that sees God in everything around it and keeps away from evil, for God is the source of spiritual enlightenment, which He gives to the eye. The eye surrounded by the bones of the face resembles Jerusalem surrounded by the mountains, illumined by the Temple that is in its midst.

17.8.0.en: 9- “From the wicked that oppress me, from my deadly enemies, who compass me about.”

17.8.1.en: Enemies of the soul: enemies of my soul.

17.8.3.en: 1- In the previous verse David showed his confidence in God's care, which is like the care of the apple of the eye and sheltering under God's wing; and here he declares that he is not disturbed by the wicked's attempt to ruin his soul, for they are worthless as long as he relies on God and takes refuge in Him. This is what happened with David when Saul's counselors incited him against David to kill him, but God was always protecting him.

17.8.4.en: 2- The hideousness of Satan's wars appears in that he wants to ruin the soul of man; therefore there is no truce with Satan, but one must keep away from every evil and every semblance of evil, because the crafty Satan presents sin in an attractive form, to make man fall into the trap.

17.8.5.en: 3- The wicked in their wickedness surround the righteous in order to make him fall; so if the righteous fortifies himself with God, in the form of spiritual practices such as prayers and fasts, he has built a wall around himself that the wicked cannot storm, for taking refuge in God is the only solution. Because of the wicked surrounding David, he pleads with God to hasten and protect him, for pleading with God is the only refuge and solution.

17.9.0.en: 10- “They are inclosed in their own fat: with their mouth they speak proudly.”

17.9.1.en: 1- David describes the wicked as having a fat heart, because they were concerned with satisfying their lusts and doing every evil, so they became extremely selfish, and consequently became unable to feel for those around them or to offer mercy and love to the needy. On the contrary, they closed their hearts and feelings to those around them.

17.9.2.en: 2- From the wicked closing their hearts we understand that a person has the freedom to feel for those around him or to refuse to; whoever is busy fattening his heart will lose his feeling for people, so that he sees their needs with his eyes and his heart is not moved to help them. And he who has closed his heart with lusts will not feel God, and consequently will not feel others. Whoever does not love God will be unable to love others.

17.9.3.en: 3- If selfishness and lusts lead to keeping away from works of mercy, they will also lead the wicked to what is worse, which is speaking with pride and troubling others, and even despising the weak. Thus we see that sin descends from the evil feelings of the heart to evil speech; whoever does not treat his inner thoughts and feelings will have evil increase within him, and it will show on his lips, and then in his deeds.

17.9.4.en: 4- This verse applies to the wicked who surrounded David, such as Saul and Absalom the son of David, and everyone who tried to wrong David. It applies also to Christ, whom the scribes, the Pharisees, the priests and the high priests tried to ensnare in a word and to deliver into the hand of the Roman authority, and then attempts to kill Him, which ended in His crucifixion; by this they closed their hearts to listening to His words, and also spoke proudly against Him.

17.10.0.en: 11- “They have now compassed us in our steps: they have set their eyes bowing down to the earth;”

17.10.1.en: Make us slip: make us fall into sin.

17.10.2.en: 1- The wicked watch the movements of the righteous at every step in order to surround him and harm him; he therefore needs God's help, which protects him and delivers him from their hands.

17.10.3.en: 2- The wicked prepare snares for us, so that we slip into them and are deceived by them, and fall into their hands, and then they laugh at us. They rejoice in evil, since they have no love; but the righteous strives to do good even to enemies, and therefore God protects him.

17.10.4.en: 3- The righteous must beware of the snares that the wicked set, which are hidden or covered with attractive things, in order to deceive the righteous by them. The remedy is prayer and careful watchfulness.

17.10.5.en: 4- If David in the previous verses spoke of the righteous in the singular, now in this verse he speaks in the plural, because Satan fights the whole Church, or the company of the righteous; it is not Christ only, but all His children.

17.10.6.en: 5- The wicked try to make us fall into earthly things, that is, earthly lusts; but if our hearts are attached to heaven, their wiles will weaken and almost come to an end, since we use earthly things as food and clothing, but our hearts are drawn to heavenly things.

17.11.0.en: 12- “Like as a lion that is greedy of his prey, and as it were a young lion lurking in secret places.”

17.11.2.en: His lair: his den, which is the lion's house.

17.11.3.en: 1- David cries out to God for help, because the wicked one who stands before him, by whom he means Satan and all who follow him, is like a lion in his strength, and this lion longs and is eager to prey upon David, since his evil nature drives him to wrong others; he loves evil and rejoices in destroying the righteous.

17.11.4.en: 2- The wicked one is also likened to a young lion: though he may seem small, he sits in his house waiting for the opportunity to crush the righteous; even if he suffers from some weakness now, he awaits the nearest opportunity to do harm to the righteous.

17.11.5.en: 3- The wicked one in his wickedness has become like the beast of prey, the lion, that is, he has gone far from God and become like an animal; he does not understand love and spiritual values, but believes only in his lusts and in fulfilling them at the expense of others.

17.11.6.en: 4- The wicked one is like the lion eager to prey upon whomever he meets. And it is known that the one who hunts is the lioness, that is, the mother who leaves her cubs in their den and goes out to prey on whatever she meets and brings the prey to be food for her mate and her young; and the lioness, in her anxiety for the young she has left at home, is fierce in her hunting, and on the other hand is seeking food for them lest they die of hunger. So the wicked one is always inclined to evil and in constant anxiety, and wrongs everyone he meets, especially the righteous, who are symbolized by tame animals.

17.11.7.en: 5- The lion is distinguished by strength and also by cunning; he seizes the opportunity to attack the last animal in a large herd so that the herd will not tear him apart, and in this he is a symbol of the wicked one who watches for the opportunity to destroy the righteous if he strays a little from the rest of the flock, that is, the members of the Church, and grows careless in his relationship with God.

17.11.8.en: If the wicked are strong and deceitful and want to devour you, do not be disturbed, for your God is stronger than they. Do not look at your weakness, but at the power of God, and you will walk in peace among the wicked, and even love them and have compassion on them, and so win them and bring them back to God by your love.

17.12.0.en: 13- “Arise, O Lord, disappoint him, cast him down: deliver my soul from the wicked, which is thy sword:”

17.12.1.en: 1- David sees that he is weak in his confrontation with Satan through the wicked who want to destroy him, so he asks God to be a barrier between him and the wicked one, just as God went before and stood between the children of Israel and the Egyptians with the pillar of fire at the Red Sea, and separated them until the people of God had crossed before Pharaoh and his army, so that they did not touch a single person of God's people and were drowned in the Red Sea (Ex 14:29). So He prevents his wrongs to David, because God is stronger than all the wicked and able to protect His children.

17.12.2.en: 2- David trusts in God's power, which is able to triumph and destroy Satan, that is, to subdue him and protect God's children from him. Thus evil returns upon the head of the wicked one, so that instead of his casting down the righteous, God casts him down. David here does not want vengeance on the wicked one, but vengeance on evil and the exposure of its vanity, to establish the faith of God's children.

17.12.3.en: 3- David asks God to deliver him by His sword, which is the word of God, which satisfies the righteous and at the same time judges the wicked and condemns them and destroys them if they do not repent.

17.12.4.en: 4- The wicked think that God's long-suffering means His neglect of men, or His weakness; therefore David calls upon God to arise, that is, to show His power, in order to stop the wicked from persisting in their wickedness, and to save his soul and all the righteous.

17.12.5.en: 5- If God's sword is meant to be the word of God, it also symbolizes His authority and justice, as well as His wrath, as it declares the truth against the vanities of the wicked. And if God is silent for a time, it is to give the wicked an opportunity to repent, but He will certainly use His sword to destroy those who oppose Him, who want to destroy the righteous.

17.13.0.en: 14- “From men which are thy hand, O Lord, from men of the world, which have their portion in this life, and whose belly thou fillest with thy hid treasure: they are full of children, and leave the rest of their substance to their babes.”

17.13.2.en: 1- David affirms his need of God to deliver him from the hands of men, the people of the world, that is, the wicked around him; he trusts in God's hand, which is able to protect him however many his enemies may be.

17.13.3.en: 2- The wicked have as their portion their earthly lusts, which they obtain during their life on earth. But the portion of the righteous is God, with whom they live on earth, until He takes them with Him into the heavenly Kingdom.

17.13.4.en: 3- The wicked forget that God is the source of all the blessings they enjoy, of food or drink or possessions, so they do not thank Him, but rise up against His righteous children to destroy them.

17.13.5.en: 4- Among God's gifts to men is that He gives them children, and also gives them material blessings with which to be satisfied and to give the remainder to their children, so that they too are satisfied. In all this they do not ascribe the glory to God, and do not thank Him, and here the selfishness of the wicked appears, for they are satisfied first and then give to their children, and this conflicts with self-giving love.

17.13.6.en: 5- God's hand symbolizes His tangible work among men, and the clearest picture of His work is His Incarnation to redeem mankind. David longs for the redemption of Christ, and speaks of it in the spirit of prophecy, that mankind may be delivered from the dominion of Satan.

17.13.7.en: 6- The wicked, to whom God gave many treasures, are still in their wickedness wanting to prey upon others; they do not need to prey, for they are satisfied, but their love of evil drives them to it.

17.13.8.en: 7- The wicked leaving their remainder to their children teaches the children the lust to prey and to destroy others, so they become wicked like their fathers. And this is the extreme of spiritual folly, that a man corrupts his children while he thinks it benefits them.

17.14.0.en: 15- “As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness.”

17.14.1.en: 1- On the other hand, the righteous walks in an upright life with God, and by this uprightness and righteousness God rejoices in him, and reveals to him His secrets and His knowledge, so that he enjoys the sight of God. This is the Kingdom on earth which, if a person lives it, qualifies him for the heavenly Kingdom. And the more a person walks in righteousness, the more he discovers God in His works and sees Him clearly in all that is around him.

17.14.2.en: 2- When a person beholds God, his heart is filled with the fear and love of Him, so he keeps away from evil and turns to good, that is, he grows in righteousness every day.

17.14.3.en: 3- The righteous cannot begin his day except with prayer, to see God, so that he longs to be like Him in his works all day long. And when he becomes like God he rejoices and is satisfied spiritually with God's love, and God also suffices him in all his bodily needs.

17.14.4.en: 4- Perfect righteousness is Christ, who lived without sin on earth: “No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him” (Jn 1:18). Through Christ the Righteous we can see God the Father, and Christ declared this clearly when He said, “without me ye can do nothing” (Jn 15:5), and we end the Lord's Prayer in Christ Jesus, through whom we receive all our requests. And the most important request is that we see God, for if we see God our souls are satisfied, and we keep striving all our lives to be like Him, until we see Him always before us. And in the end we reach the Kingdom through the righteousness He has given us on earth. And there we see none but God, the everlasting satisfaction forever. From this we understand that this verse is a prophecy about Christ.

17.14.5.en: 5- Righteousness is purity of heart, and Christ declared in His Sermon on the Mount, saying, “Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God” (Mt 5:8); so in righteousness we behold the face of God.

17.14.6.en: 6- If the wicked are satisfied with the lusts of the world and do not perceive God who gives them (v. 15), the righteous are satisfied by seeing God and being like Him, and they see that all the material things in their hands are a grace from God and speak to them of Him.

17.14.7.en: 7- The righteous in righteousness beholds God all day long, and at night sees God in his dreams, and when he awakes longs to be like God in his thoughts, his speech and his conduct.

17.14.8.en: 8- David concludes the Psalm by saying that the life of the righteous is in seeing God always through his continual prayer. And if he is distracted from God, he returns and takes heed and awakes from his heedlessness, and sees God and is satisfied with Him, and in his life is like God, that is, a true human being as God wants him, who created him in His image and likeness. And if he falls into sin he rises from it with the risen Christ, and returns and beholds God and enjoys Him.

17.14.9.en: Your life is God, and you can taste Him and behold Him through prayer; so never keep away from it, but seek God at all times, not only in your official times of prayer, but before every work and during it and after it, and you will enjoy seeing Him.

17.14.10.en: God is my deliverer and my strength. To the chief musician. For the servant of the Lord, David, who spoke to the Lord the words of this song in the day that the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul, and he said:

17.14.11.en: “I will love thee, O Lord, my strength” (v. 1). Introduction:

17.14.12.en: 1- Its writer: David, as we find in the title of this Psalm.

17.14.13.en: 2- When it was said: there are two opinions:

17.14.14.en: A- The title of this Psalm mentions that David said it on the day God delivered him from his enemies. By the day is meant the end of the troubles David faced from Saul and many enemies, such as Ishbi-benob (2 Sam 21:15-17); this period in his view was as one day, and he accepted the sufferings for God's sake, who saved him, and he is in joy and thanks God for delivering him; that is, David wrote it at the end of his life, and this is the more probable opinion.

17.14.15.en: B- The other opinion is that David did not write this Psalm at the end of his life, but wrote it after he reigned over the whole kingdom of the children of Israel, when the wars of Saul were still clear in his mind, and before he suffered the fall of adultery and murder; because he speaks much of his righteousness and perfection, that is, he had not yet reached the age of forty.

17.14.16.en: 3- This Psalm is found almost word for word in (2 Sam 22). From this it is clear that it was said at the end of his life, that is, about thirty years after he began to reign.

17.14.17.en: 4- In the introduction to this Psalm David calls himself the servant of the Lord, and this shows his humility and his pride in belonging to God and relying on Him.

17.14.18.en: 5- This Psalm is one of the Messianic Psalms, for it speaks many prophecies about Christ.

17.14.19.en: 6- The Apostle Paul quoted from this Psalm twice, namely (Rom 15:9; Heb 2:13).

17.14.20.en: 7- God's delivering David from his enemies is a symbol of Christ's victory over Satan by the Cross and His Resurrection, and then His reign forever.

17.14.21.en: 8- This Psalm suits everyone who strives in his spiritual life, strengthening him and establishing his hope of victory.

17.14.22.en: 9- In the Septuagint translation we find in the title of the Psalm “to the end,” by which is meant:

17.14.23.en: A- the complete deliverance of David from his enemies and his rest as king.

17.14.24.en: B- a prophecy about the completion of salvation on the Cross.

17.14.25.en: C- a prophecy about the acceptance of the Gentiles, that is, the offering of redemption to mankind, to the whole world.

17.14.26.en: 10- David spoke this song to the Lord, as appears in the title of the Psalm, and it does not say that he praised or sang it; he said it without musical instruments, and it seems that this was because of his advanced age, so that he did not chant the Psalm with melodies or music.

17.14.27.en: 11- This Psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
